title: Sturge-Weber Syndrome: Encephalotrigeminal Angiomatosis
summary: A rare phakomatosis characterized by a triad of facial port-wine stains, leptomeningeal angiomas, and ocular involvement, most notably glaucoma. Proper management requires a multidisciplinary approach focused on intraocular pressure control and neuro-developmental support.

sections.title: Definition & Pathophysiology
sections.content: SWS is a non-hereditary neurocutaneous disorder caused by a somatic activating mutation in the GNAQ gene (c.548G>A; p.Arg183Gln). This leads to abnormal capillary venous malformations in the distribution of the trigeminal nerve (V1/V2) and the ipsilateral leptomeninges, resulting in impaired venous drainage, cortical ischemia, and elevated episcleral venous pressure.

sections.title: Clinical Features Checklist
content: Port-wine stain (Nevus flammeus) involving V1 distribution

sections.title: Red Flags: Emergencies
content: Retinal detachment associated with choroidal effusion

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: Step 1: Topical anti-glaucoma medication (Prostaglandin analogues, CAIs, Beta-blockers)
Step 2: Goniotomy or Trabeculotomy (if angle dysgenesis is present)
Step 3: Trabeculectomy with Mitomycin-C or Aqueous Shunt devices

content.explanation: G: GNAQ mutation; N: Neurocutaneous; A: Angiomatosis (Leptomeningeal); Q: Query IOP early.

sections.title: Key Practice Pearls
content: Monitor for 'tomato-ketchup' fundus (diffuse red-orange choroidal hemangioma)
Risk of choroidal effusion post-trabeculectomy is significantly higher in SWS
Glaucoma is often bimodal: infancy or early adulthood
Always perform gonioscopy to differentiate primary dysgenesis from secondary causes
